source: Raby, Alexis, Dickinson, Clayton (2007) Planning for the future by western scrub-jays. Nature 445:919-921
finding: Only the abstract and figure captions are public. Jays cached more in the place where they had learned they would be hungry next morning, and spread two food types so each type would be missing at the other site next day.
numbers: No cache counts are visible without a subscription. Figure 2 caption: mean peanuts and kibble cached in the breakfast-choice experiment. Other sources give N=8 and one test evening.
quote: the jays can spontaneously plan for tomorrow without reference to their current motivational state
limits: Paywalled (subscription preview). Gap 1 stays open for Raby: exact counts and statistics were not obtained.
agent_relevance: None directly. Do not quote Raby effect sizes from this project; cite the design only.

source: Correia, Dickinson, Clayton (2007) Western scrub-jays anticipate future needs independently of their current motivational state. Curr Biol 17:856-861
finding: Full text could not be fetched: the publisher blocked automated downloads (HTML stub returned for the open PDF link; 403 on the full-text page). Design known only through Amodio 2021: a between-subjects specific-satiety design.
numbers: No counts obtained.
limits: Gap 1 stays open for Correia. Semantic Scholar lists a hybrid open-access PDF, so a browser download by a human would work.
agent_relevance: None.

source: Amodio et al. (2021) Testing two competing hypotheses for Eurasian jays' caching for the future. Sci Rep (PMC7804264)
finding: Describes the Raby protocol and lists differences that could explain the split. Raby: scrub-jays housed in pairs, 2-hour experience trials, six days, each compartment always tied to one condition, one test evening. Amodio: group-housed, 15-minute trials, nine days, conditions rotated every three days.
numbers: Raby: 6 experience days then one cache evening. Amodio: 9 experience days then one test trial.
quote: A crucial step for future research is to replicate the findings reported here in Eurasian jays, and those obtained by Raby et al.
limits: Authors say the results cannot show why the studies disagree. Different species and a harder, rotating design. They call for a replication of Raby itself.
agent_relevance: Shows that the key jay result depends on a stable place-need link; an agent test should vary stability on purpose.

source: Martin, Martin, Roberts, Sherry (2021) No evidence for future planning in Canada jays. Biol Lett (PMC8651407)
finding: Closest published re-run of the Raby breakfast design. Same steps except food items and a 1-hour shift in light times. Birds were wild-caught, in captivity 8-18 months, with prior caching experience, and the study repeated the breakfast step three times.
numbers: N=6 Canada jays. They cached more where they had found food (opposite to Raby). Breakfast choice: 3 of 6 did not cache; the other 3 averaged six caches (bird 1: 2 same, 1 different; bird 2: 4 vs 8; bird 3: 3 vs 0).
limits: Different species; authors say history of the birds may matter (captive scrub-jays had long caching experience). Tiny N. Not a same-species replication.
agent_relevance: None. Supports the claim that the jay result is fragile, not that it is false.

source: Farrar, Boeckle, Clayton (2020) Replications in Comparative Cognition: What Should We Expect and How Can We Improve? Anim Behav Cogn (PMC7334049)
finding: Direct replication is often impossible in this field. The authors give their own case: the Cambridge lab no longer houses California scrub-jays, so replication there is very unlikely. Only one other lab (Clary et al. 2019) was publishing on scrub-jay caching.
numbers: No data. Argues published effects are overestimated and that tiny N makes original and replication hard to tell apart.
quote: the possibility of these studies being directly replicated with California scrub-jays in this lab in the coming years is very low
limits: Written 2020; a later multi-lab scrub-jay replication may exist but none was found in Europe PMC title searches or reference lists read.
agent_relevance: For gap 2: no large-N or pre-registered western scrub-jay replication of Raby was found; the structural reason is that the original lab lost the birds.

source: Boeckle et al. (2021) New Caledonian crows' planning behaviour: a reply to de Mahy et al. Proc R Soc B (PMC8437238)
finding: Authors answer the critique that crows might solve the spoon test by association. They say the test pits a tool tied to past reward (stick) against a tool never rewarded after seeing that apparatus, so past reward does not explain a correct choice. They state no new data and make no claim about a concept of the future.
numbers: Same design as Boeckle 2020: apparatus seen, 5 min later a 5-object choice, 10 min later access to the apparatus. No new birds.
limits: An exchange, not a replication. As of this search no second lab or extra crows had been reported; Europe PMC searches found only this reply and the comment.
agent_relevance: For gap 9: the spoon result stands unreplicated; training-history control is argued, not tested.

source: Bugaud (2026) CheeseBench v1 (arXiv 2604.10825v1)
finding: Version 1 (12 Apr 2026) tested six open-weight models only. Best was Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
numbers: 52.6% average success (ASCII) vs 32.1% random vs 78.9% rodent reference.
limits: The arXiv abstract page labelled v2 still shows these v1 numbers (stale abstract).
agent_relevance: Settles gap 7 on versions: the 52.6/32.1 pair belongs to v1.

source: Bugaud (2026) CheeseBench v2 (arXiv 2604.10825v2, 15 May 2026), frontier models
finding: Version 2 re-ran with a new random baseline and added seven frontier models. Frontier models reach or pass the rodent reference. The radial-arm maze, near zero for open-weight models, is solved by the top Claude models but not by GPT-4.1.
numbers: Best open-weight 68.0% vs random 38.0% vs rodent 78.9%. Overall: Opus 4.7 86.7, GPT-5.2-Codex 82.2, Opus 4.6 82.2, Sonnet 4.6 81.1, GPT-5.2 75.6, Haiku 4.5 70.0, GPT-4.1 55.6. Radial arm maze: Opus 4.7 100%, Opus 4.6 90%, GPT-4.1 0%, open-weight best 10%. Frontier runs used 10 trials per environment (270 per model; 81 for GPT-4.1).
limits: Wide confidence intervals at 10 trials per cell. Frontier numbers are best of three view modes. Single author, preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 closed: use v2 (68.0/38.0, frontier table). The radial-arm gap does close for Claude Opus models, so working-memory tracking is not a hard limit for strong models.

source: Bei et al. (2026) Prospective Memory for Proactive LLM Agents (Pro-Memory), arXiv 2611.05731, main results
finding: A memory with pending intentions, activation conditions and states beats retrospective memories on two benchmarks (PM-Bench and ProactiveBench) across five backbones, including Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5.
numbers: PM-Bench Set-F1, no memory to Pro-Memory: Sonnet 4.5 0.5224 to 0.7600 (best baseline RWM 0.7273); Haiku 4.5 0.4561 to 0.7324 (RWM 0.6479); Kimi-K2.5 0.5175 to 0.7619; GLM-4.7 0.4219 to 0.7068 (RWM 0.7218 higher). ProactiveBench F1 Sonnet 0.7376, Haiku 0.6634. Pro-Memory range across backbones 0.7007-0.7619.
limits: Authors' own method, preprint (3 Nov 2026), small test set (PM-Bench has about 81 positive items by the hit rates). GLM-4.7 PM-Bench was won by the baseline RWM.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a typed intention ledger does hold on a second benchmark and with Claude models. Supports an explicit pending-intention list in the schema.

source: Bei et al. (2026) Pro-Memory, retrospective memory and cost analysis
finding: Retrospective memory can hurt proactive behaviour. Removing links between intentions and evidence raises false alarms. Pro-Memory also cost fewer tokens than the next-best baseline.
numbers: Haiku 4.5 ProactiveBench F1: no memory 0.5103; RAG 0.3636; A-Mem 0.3276; T-Mem 0.3248. Ablation on Haiku: w/o evidence links lowers Set-F1 by 8.45 points and more than doubles false-alarm rate; w/o maintenance -2.17 (Sonnet), -1.91 (Haiku). Tokens for a full PM-Bench run: Pro-Memory 1.61M (Sonnet), 1.10M (Haiku); RWM uses 1.28x and 1.91x as many; T-Mem 21.8x and 26.3x.
limits: Token totals are for a whole evaluation, not per item. Self-reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 (cost): the ledger approach is not token-heavy. Plain retrieval can lower proactive accuracy, so do not assume memory helps.

source: Xu et al. (2026) ProMemAgent and CPMBench, arXiv 2610.27400
finding: Prospective-memory agent over egocentric audio and video, with cue-triggered retrieval and cross-event linking. Each memory part helps.
numbers: CPMBench (1,000 instances, 8 categories): ProMemAgent Set-F1 75.2, direct-QA Recall@10 98.1. Removing cross-event linking drops Set-F1 to 65.9; removing another part drops it to 32.3. On the noisy CPMBench-Omni it beats full-context GPT-5.4 by 10.3 Set-F1 points. Direct-QA recall falls from 98.1 to 70.0 without content retrieval.
limits: Uses a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B reasoner; authors' own benchmark; not a Claude test. Ablation column labels were lost in text extraction, so which part gives 65.9 versus 32.3 is not certain.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a third, independent-group benchmark where cue plus link memory beats full context.

source: Zhao and Wu (2026) Typed Intention Stores for Small-Model Agents (PIS), arXiv 2609.01272
finding: A code-side intention lifecycle with scoped model calls lets small models do PM-Bench. Abstract page only; full text not parsed.
numbers: DeepSeek-Chat 82.9% Set-F1 on PM-Bench. Gemma-E2B 4.2% without a store, at most 6.6% with seven retrospective memories, 66.2% with PIS. A second figure of 70.1% vs at most 54.4% for retrospective methods is stated without naming the setting.
limits: Abstract only. Same benchmark as the original, so it is not an independent benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: ledger logic in code beats prompts for small models.

source: Groff (2026) Memory That Looks Forward: A Zero-Inference Prospective Term for Personal Memory Retrieval, arXiv 2609.22091
finding: A dated or trigger-conditioned commitment ledger boosts retrieval of linked items. Tested on a synthetic set modelled on TriggerBench, not on TriggerBench itself.
numbers: 48 dialogues, 175 tasks. Hard stratum recall@5 0.000 to 0.955 (1.000 with a floor variant). Zero false boosts across 53 resolved-commitment tasks. Only 17-29% of naturally phrased commitment-trigger pairs defeat embedding similarity.
limits: Author-built set, preliminary; the author says TriggerBench proper is future work.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a ledger helps on the minority of hard cases and does no harm elsewhere, in this small test.

source: Mittal et al. (2026) arXiv 2603.23530, task accuracy under formatting constraint plus reminder (Table 3)
finding: The reminder that restores constraint compliance has a cost on the main task, strongest for the reasoning model o4-mini on chained maths.
numbers: Task-only accuracy: GSM8K single o4-mini 93.3, DeepSeek 87.8, Llama 94.4. With constraint plus reminder: GSM8K x3 o4-mini 26.7, DeepSeek 76.7, Llama 64.4; x5 o4-mini 53.7, DeepSeek 77.8, Llama 61.1; MMLU o4-mini 82.2 to 76.5. max_tokens 2048, greedy, 90 items per condition (270 for GSM8K).
limits: No token-cost figure is given for the reminder itself. o4-mini output was capped at 2048 completion tokens, which may truncate reasoning. Only three models, none a recent frontier model.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: reminders trade main-task accuracy for compliance in a reasoning model; test the reminder on the real task, not on compliance alone.

source: TriggerBench (arXiv 2606.23459) Table 3, strong reasoning models at base and 40K context
finding: Strong reasoning models hold prospective memory far better than non-reasoning ones, but also lose accuracy as context grows, and trade recall for false reminders.
numbers: Overall PM Acc at base context: Qwen3-235B-Think 74.86, GPT-4.1 60.00, GPT-4o 51.78, Qwen3-32B 40.71. At 40K context: GPT-5.2 (high) 75.02 with negative-clean 39.80; Qwen3-235B-Think 52.65; GPT-4.1 45.22; Qwen3-235B-Inst 40.71; RAG baseline 38.26.
limits: The table is read from flattened text; column headers are lost, so which column is overall is inferred from the earlier cross-check (c10). Treat the 40K row labels as likely, not certain.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: effort level buys robustness at long context, but false alarms stay high (a 39.80 negative-clean score for GPT-5.2).

source: Meta-analysis (J Exp Psychol Gen 2022) Promoting farsighted decisions via episodic future thinking, abstract record and OSF preprint record
finding: Abstract text in Europe PMC (PMID 34843367) matches the earlier line b19. Also says the analysis included many unpublished experiments and that the effect was robust to publication-bias adjustment and unlikely to reflect demand characteristics.
numbers: 174 effect sizes, 48 articles, g=0.44, 95% CI [0.33, 0.55]. Moderators: more positive, more vivid, related to the delayed choice; larger in impulsive samples.
limits: Full text not read: the OSF download was an image-only PDF with no extractable text. Gap 6 only partly closed (abstract-level confirmation).
agent_relevance: Moderators that plausibly carry to an LLM prompt: concrete detail and link to the choice at hand. Positive valence, vividness and impulsivity have no clear LLM analogue.

source: Meta-analysis of the effects of episodic future thinking on delay discounting (Q J Exp Psychol 2022), abstract record
finding: Abstract text in Europe PMC (PMID 34841982) matches line b20. Authors note earlier results were inconsistent.
numbers: 47 studies, 63 contrasts, g=0.52. Positive EFT 0.64, valence not stated 0.28, neutral or negative -0.03. Control task and discounting task features also moderated the effect.
limits: Abstract only. The two meta-analyses use different samples, so g 0.44 and 0.52 are not independent confirmations of each other.
agent_relevance: Both agree on direction and concreteness. Neither measures plan quality.

source: Manakina et al. (2026) Delay-of-Gratification as a Multi-Agent Survival Micro-benchmark for Long-Horizon LLMs, arXiv 2609.29509
finding: Nearest LLM test of a delay-of-gratification (marshmallow) paradigm. ReAct agents wait minute by minute. Abstract page only.
numbers: 19,200 trajectories, 64 cells. 75.9% of agents persist to the end. Mandatory self-questioning raised risk of giving in; isolation lowered it. Mean 7.12 questions. Removing hedonic drive and persona age gives completion near 1.0.
limits: Persona prompts supply the drive, so it is role play, not a state the agent has. Not a caching or future-need choice. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: closest adjacent test; shows waiting can be manipulated by prompt. It does not test choosing for a future state different from the current one.

source: Search record: LLM tests of caching, future-need choice, Bischof-Kohler or hunger-state hoarding (arXiv listing searches, 19 Nov 2026)
finding: Searches for Bischof-Kohler, future need caching LLM agent hunger, mental time travel large language models and foresight or anticipatory planning returned no study that tests caching for a different future need. Hits were the Poonsiriwong avatar study, CheeseBench and the delay-of-gratification benchmark. Later queries were blocked by rate limits.
numbers: 0 direct hits across about 10 arXiv listing queries. Web search was not available (budget exhausted).
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search. Listing search is keyword-based and can miss papers that use other words.
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 10 stay open. This would be a new experiment: give an agent hunger and location states and score by the Amodio model set.

source: Ahmadi et al. (2025) AI-Facilitated Episodic Future Thinking For Adults with Obesity (EFTeacher), arXiv 2503.16484
finding: A GPT-4-Turbo chatbot that writes episodic-future-thinking cues was judged usable and supportive. It measured usability and interviews only, not delay discounting.
numbers: Mixed-methods feasibility study; no discounting outcome reported on the abstract page. Users noted repetitive and verbose dialogue.
limits: Abstract only. Feasibility study, not an efficacy test.
agent_relevance: No evidence yet that LLM-written EFT cues change choices; links to K11 only through the human meta-analyses.

source: Su (2026) Learning Situation-Conditioned Thinking Policies for Long-Term LLM Agents, arXiv 2610.09590
finding: A lightweight learned policy predicts what to think about in a situation, includes future-thinking accuracy. Abstract page only.
numbers: DeepSeek reasoning F1 0.789 to 0.868; 1.000 F1 on temporal-rule generalization; future-thinking accuracy 1.000 after enough repeated cross-experience evidence; query time 0.3636 ms to 0.0382 ms at 30,000 situations.
limits: Synthetic rule-based tasks; single author; abstract only. The perfect scores suggest an easy task.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: not an equal-token test of a prospection step; no such test was found.
